speaker: stephenraitz
text: All right, good evening, Your Worship and Council. I'll just be sharing my screen with a presentation to support the report that we're bringing forward. So, that should be visible now. And I'm assuming I'm coming through clearly. Yes, we have you. Excellent, all right. So, administration will present its findings and recommendations for the election signage regulations. And then at the end of this presentation, we'll open to questions of administration from Council. And so, this presentation is focused on bringing forward the recommendation that Council direct administration to make the recommended changes cited within this report to regulate election signage by using the appropriate enforcement mechanisms and bylaws to be adopted by Council prior to January 1st, 2021. So, to provide some context, at this point in time, election signage regulations are primarily regulated within the Land Use Bylaw. And so, although this bylaw was updated in 2019 on a pretty holistic basis, the regulations focused on election signage regulations have been in place since 1997 and were just transferred from the previous bylaw to this bylaw. And so, these regulations haven't been in place since 1997. However, we do recognize that election periods mark a temporary departure from the normal types and the amounts of signage that we see in the community. So, we've developed some recommendations to ameliorate concerns that may arise due to this sort of temporary departure from the normal sort of types and amounts of signage present within the community. And so, in doing this, we are focused on three concerns, three purposes here on safety to ensure that sight lines and traffic can safely navigate the transportation system. We're focused on providing a clear process and standardization for those who are putting up signs. And then, we're also trying to limit aesthetic impacts to the community, avoiding visual noise and those sorts of components that may arise or be perceived to arise during municipal election periods or any election periods for that purpose. And so, the research that was undertaken for this was a legislative review, which found that there were not any significant sort of directions or impediments on how we would be attempting to regulate election signage going forward based on these recommendations. And then, we also reviewed provincial regulations, which focused on provincial highways that can be incorporated and followed through the recommended approach. And then, we completed a scan of municipalities to see what their approach would be to inform our own decisions going forward. And so, we looked at nine municipalities in total, some in the region and some across Canada. And so, we found a couple of different approaches. The, some municipalities will have an entire signage bylaw that will regulate all forms of signage. Smaller municipalities like the city of Beaumont regulate signage within the land use bylaw primarily. And then, the city of Edmonton option, which is how the recommended approach would have election signage regulations being present in a few different bylaws to ensure it's being enforced in the correct approaches. However, these are then pulled out into a set of guidelines that are easily conveyed to candidates and that candidates can agree to follow going forward. And so, that would be our recommended approach. And then, the actual things that we were hoping to regulate fall into these sort of categories to ensure that we're achieving those three purposes of safety, standardization, and limiting aesthetic impacts. And so, this includes timelines for removal, placement requirements, clear definitions, distance requirements, and prohibiting certain forms of signage. And so, these were all the different areas that other municipalities were regulating. And we, the administration has identified that based on our current regulations and what we are hoping to achieve, there are just a few of these that we need to focus in on. And so, this would include timelines for removal. This actually expands the amount of time that signage would be up for after the election. However, this would be in alignment with other jurisdictions in the area. And one just ensures some coherence based on what people may be hearing from neighbors. Altering this from 48 hours to 72 hours, this would give candidates more time to clear election signage after the election period is over. So, it would be shifting from two days to three days, basically. Now, we shipped into requirements that would more substantially impact how election signage can be placed. And so, the regulations focusing on placement requirements, we are able to prohibit signage being placed in specific locations. This would include school zones and playground zones. That would be coming from sort of a safety perspective to ensure that in these areas where we may see more pedestrian traffic, more traffic at certain times of the day, that election signage does not overpopulate or become a distraction in those areas. And then additionally, making it explicitly clear that signage cannot be present on roadway medians would be a way to ensure safety through limiting impediments to sight lines while in transit or moving. And so, this would also provide clear process for everyone. This can be very easily visually displayed on a map of where signs can and cannot be placed, and then would also fit the purpose of reducing visual clutter. Other municipalities also regulate distance requirements. And so, this is somewhere that the city of Beaumont does not currently regulate, but can regulate if these recommended changes are moved forward on. We have identified 15 or 1.5 meters as a clear basis of separation in a couple of different scenarios, requiring 15 meters from basically any intersection, crosswalk and fire hydrant. This again is to ensure safety, reduce visual cluttering, provide a clear process. Also requiring 1.5 meters from the edge of the curb of a roadway for similar reasons. And then finally requiring 15 meters separation between two signs of a single candidate. So, these all require that signs not be placed in these areas or must meet these thresholds basically, and can be pretty easily conveyed again through the guidelines that would be developed after amending the appropriate bylaws to enforce these mechanisms. And then the final piece, we did identify that some municipalities provide a distinct definition for election signage. Currently, what we are operating on within the city of Beaumont, we identified as strong enough and we could maintain the current maximum of 0.6 meters squared. This would, we don't feel we have to go beyond this in any ways, with 0.6 meters squared is pretty stringent as is, and still allows candidates to be placing signage out in the community that is visible and allows them to participate in the election, but also would ensure that we don't see strange forms of signage that usually need to be larger in scope. So, we can basically work with the definition that we have right now. So, looking at next steps, based on the recommendation that administration has brought forward, what administration would plan to do if council provides direction for, would be to develop the set of amendments to impacted bylaws, which could include the land use bylaw, the traffic safety bylaw, et cetera. And then based on these amendments being created and passed, we would be able to create a set of guidelines for candidates to follow for the 2021 municipal election. And this would be the process that we would work through if council provides direction for this. And so this would conclude the presentation from administration and we'll welcome any questions from council at this point.
